title: The map
lede: All 130 legal ideas the project holds and the 124 provisions they cite, drawn as the network they are. **52 of the ideas were signed by a named person; 78 were written by a machine and nobody has read them** — and the picture says which is which on every node. It opens on **one concept and what it is joined to**: double-click a node to open it and draw its neighbours, drag any node to move it, and click one to read the passage its record quotes. *Show the whole map* draws all of it at once, which is the honest picture of a graph in pieces and not a way to answer a question about one idea.

items.label: Provisions they cite
items.note: at the address the record uses, never rolled up

items.label: Edges
items.note: each one a field in a record, not an inference

nodes.label: connotation
nodes.notes: The Manual states that for section 43 the term has a wider meaning than the dictionary sense and includes direct statements. That widening is a practice position, and whether it survives into the ontology as one concept or two is a judgement.

quote.text: If there is doubt that a connotation exists, then the ground for rejection should not be raised.
quote.from: the evidence for the group it was sorted into

typing.meaning: a question the decision maker has to answer

authored.reasoning: Section 43 makes rejection turn on there being a connotation, and Part 29.2.4 makes its existence something the Registrar has to be satisfied about before the ground is raised — doubt defeats it. A matter the decision maker must answer is a legal_test on the owner's four groups, so connotation is typed as the first of section 43's two elements rather than as material feeding into one.
authored.expert_should_check: Whether the existence of a connotation is genuinely a separate question from whether the mark is likely to deceive, or whether practice runs the two together. GC-0002 is typed legal_test on the same footing, and if they are one question the pair should collapse into it.
alternatives_considered: relevant_factor — a connotation is also the thing found in a mark, and everything from a place name to an INN stem feeds into whether one exists. That would be the right reading if the four groups sorted concepts by what they are rather than by the part they play in the decision; it would also leave section 43's first element with no test.
ground_of_refusal — rejected because a connotation on its own refuses nothing. The Manual is explicit that a connotation must additionally be likely to deceive or confuse.

evidence.quote: If there is doubt that a connotation exists, then the ground for rejection should not be raised.

If the trade mark, or some part of the trade mark, contains a connotation that would be likely to deceive or confuse consumers within the relevant market, then a ground for rejection should be raised.

nodes.label: likely to deceive or cause confusion
not: likelihood of confusion between trade marks
nodes.notes: Whether this should be one concept or two is a real question. The Manual quotes Lord Denning distinguishing them sharply, then applies them as a single threshold. We have kept them together with the two narrower concepts underneath; splitting them is a defensible correction.

quote.text: it is necessary for a decision maker to be clearly satisfied that use of the trade mark for the specified goods and / or services would be likely to deceive or cause confusion
quote.from: the evidence for the group it was sorted into

typing.meaning: a question the decision maker has to answer

authored.reasoning: The Manual states this as the thing a decision maker must be clearly satisfied of, which is the definition of a question the decision maker has to answer. Every other concept in the s 43 vocabulary either feeds this question or takes a case out of it.
authored.expert_should_check: The split between this record and GT-0006. If 'ground for rejection' and 'likely to deceive or cause confusion' name the same thing in practice, one of the two typings is wrong and the vocabulary has a duplicate underneath it.
alternatives_considered: ground_of_refusal — the phrase is the operative words of the statutory ground, and an expert may prefer to type the ground where the Act puts it rather than splitting it into elements. GC-0006 carries ground_of_refusal in this pass, so taking that reading would make one of the two redundant.

evidence.quote: it is necessary for a decision maker to be clearly satisfied that use of the trade mark for the specified goods and / or services would be likely to deceive or cause confusion

nodes.label: deception
nodes.notes: "Misdescriptive" is listed as an alt label on the strength of one passage. It may be a related but distinct idea rather than a synonym.

quote.text: When you deceive a man, you tell him a lie.
quote.from: the evidence for the group it was sorted into

typing.meaning: a question the decision maker has to answer

authored.reasoning: Typed as a limb of GC-0002 rather than as an input to it. The Manual quotes Lord Denning distinguishing deception from confusion sharply and then says the connotation must be judged as giving rise to one or the other — so each limb is a question that can be answered on its own.
authored.expert_should_check: Whether an examiner ever decides deception and confusion separately, or whether the distinction is quoted for colour and applied as a single threshold. GC-0002's own record note raises this and it is unresolved.
alternatives_considered: relevant_factor — right if deception and confusion are two ways of describing one threshold rather than two questions, which is how the rest of Part 29 applies them.
none_of_these — right if 'deception' here is a description of an effect rather than anything the decision maker decides.

evidence.quote: When you deceive a man, you tell him a lie.
Importantly it must be judged as giving rise to deception and / or confusion.

nodes.label: confusion
nodes.notes: "Caused to wonder" comes from a passage quoted from a decision under earlier legislation. Whether it is a synonym or a test is a reading.

quote.text: But you may cause confusion without telling him a lie at all, and without making any false representation to him.
quote.from: the evidence for the group it was sorted into

typing.meaning: a question the decision maker has to answer

authored.reasoning: The mirror of GT-0003, and typed the same way for the same reason: confusion has its own threshold in the corpus — persons caused to wonder, a reasonable doubt entertained — which is a question with an answer rather than a consideration that feeds one.
authored.expert_should_check: The same question as GT-0003, and it should be answered for both at once. If the pair collapse into GC-0002, this record and GT-0003 both become relevant_factor or disappear.
alternatives_considered: relevant_factor — as for GT-0003, right if the two limbs are one threshold.
none_of_these — right if confusion is the effect and the test is only 'likely to deceive or cause confusion' as a whole.

evidence.quote: But you may cause confusion without telling him a lie at all, and without making any false representation to him.
it is sufficient if the result of the user of the mark will be that a number of persons will be caused to wonder

nodes.label: denotation
nodes.notes: The Manual gives the denotation of a mark as the connection in trade between the applicant and the goods or services.

quote.text: a distinction is to be made between the denotation of the mark and its connotation
quote.from: the evidence for the group it was sorted into

typing.meaning: something that feeds into that answer

authored.reasoning: Separating what a mark denotes from what it connotes is a step in reaching the connotation finding, so denotation feeds the answer rather than being one. It is typed relevant_factor on that basis and not on the basis that anybody weighs it.
authored.expert_should_check: Whether denotation does any work of its own in an examination, or whether it appears only in the case law the Manual quotes. If the latter, none_of_these is the better answer and this record is the clearest example of the four groups not fitting.
alternatives_considered: none_of_these — the stronger alternative. Denotation is a definitional foil the Manual uses to say what connotation is not; a foil is not a factor, and if the four groups are about what the decision maker weighs, this belongs outside them.

evidence.quote: a distinction is to be made between the denotation of the mark and its connotation
The operative test is the secondary meaning which arises from the reasonable expectations of the consumer after considering the meaning in the context of the goods.

nodes.label: ground for rejection
nodes.notes: The Manual uses "objection" and "ground for rejection" interchangeably in places. If they are not interchangeable in practice, that is a correction with consequences across the whole entity set.

quote.text: the trade mark is registrable provided none of the grounds referred to in sections 39 to 44 of the Act are found to apply
quote.from: the evidence for the group it was sorted into

typing.meaning: a reason an application can be refused

authored.reasoning: The only concept in the 52 that names a reason an application can be refused rather than something inside the reasoning, and its alt label 's 43 objection' ties it to the concrete ground rather than to the abstract category. Typed ground_of_refusal so the group is not empty on a vocabulary built entirely around one ground.
authored.expert_should_check: Whether the vocabulary needs 'ground for rejection' (the general notion) and 'section 43 ground for rejection' (the particular one) as two concepts. This record types them as one, which is the reason the ground_of_refusal group has exactly one member in 52.
alternatives_considered: none_of_these — the serious alternative. This concept names the taxonomy's own category, so typing it ground_of_refusal makes the class a member of itself. That would be right if the vocabulary is expected to grow a separate concept for the section 43 ground specifically.

evidence.quote: the trade mark is registrable provided none of the grounds referred to in sections 39 to 44 of the Act are found to apply
then a ground for rejection should be raised

nodes.label: presumption of registrability
nodes.notes: The not_label is a live one: a passage quoted in 29.3.1 places the onus on the applicant, in the context of earlier legislation. Whether the two sit together is a legal question, not a drafting one.

quote.text: The presumption of registrability applies to section 43.
quote.from: the evidence for the group it was sorted into

typing.meaning: something that takes a case out of the rule

authored.reasoning: Typed on what the presumption does rather than on what it is. Its stated operation in Part 29 is that doubt about a connotation stops the ground being raised — a case that might otherwise attract the ground is taken out of it, which is the exception group's definition.
authored.expert_should_check: This record and GT-0051. GC-0007's own note says the presumption and the mandatory application of s 43 pull in opposite directions; they are typed here as exception and none_of_these respectively, and if that is the wrong pairing both are wrong together.
alternatives_considered: legal_test — the presumption is really a standard of satisfaction ('the Registrar must be satisfied that a ground for rejection exists'), and a standard is a question, not an out. This is the reading to prefer if the exception group is meant for substantive carve-outs rather than for burden rules.
none_of_these — right if a burden of proof is simply a different kind of thing from the four groups.

evidence.quote: The presumption of registrability applies to section 43.
If there is doubt that a connotation exists, then the ground for rejection should not be raised.

nodes.label: real and tangible danger
nodes.notes: The not_labels are both phrases the Manual uses to say what the test is *not*, which makes them unusually well-evidenced near-misses.

quote.text: There must be a real and obvious danger of the buying public being deceived and/or confused by the secondary meaning within the trade mark. A possibility of confusion or a suggestion that deception might occur is not sufficient.
quote.from: the evidence for the group it was sorted into

typing.meaning: a question the decision maker has to answer

authored.reasoning: The corpus states this as a threshold with a floor under it — a mere possibility will not do — which makes it a question with a yes or no answer rather than a consideration. It is the level at which GC-0002 is set, not a separate ground.
authored.expert_should_check: Whether this is a second test or the calibration of GC-0002's single test. If the latter, the two records should say so rather than both carrying legal_test as though they were independent questions.
alternatives_considered: relevant_factor — right if 'real and tangible danger' is treated as the way the deception question is described rather than as a distinct step in answering it.

evidence.quote: There must be a real and obvious danger of the buying public being deceived and/or confused by the secondary meaning within the trade mark. A possibility of confusion or a suggestion that deception might occur is not sufficient.
For a mark to be rejected under s 43 there must be a ‘real tangible danger of deception or confusion’.

nodes.label: relevant market
nodes.notes: Low confidence. These may be four distinct ideas that an examiner chooses between deliberately.

quote.text: would be likely to deceive or confuse consumers within the relevant market
quote.from: the evidence for the group it was sorted into

typing.meaning: something that feeds into that answer

authored.reasoning: Identifying whose reaction counts is an input to the deception question, not the question itself. The Manual never asks whether there is a relevant market; it asks whether that market would be deceived.
authored.expert_should_check: The line this pass drew between a population that is weighed (typed relevant_factor, as here and at GT-0010) and an actor who decides (typed none_of_these, GT-0044 to GT-0046). If that line is wrong, four records move together.
alternatives_considered: none_of_these — right if 'relevant market' is a party or population rather than a consideration, in the way GC-0044 and GC-0046 are actors and are typed none_of_these here.

evidence.quote: would be likely to deceive or confuse consumers within the relevant market
there must be some connotation within the trade mark that would reasonably be expected to cause deception or confusion in the mind of the relevant buying public

nodes.label: ordinary consumer
nodes.notes: The first not_label is the Manual's own words, quoted from a decision. It is the clearest negative boundary marker in the pilot area.

quote.text: The tests lie in the perception of the ordinary person
quote.from: the evidence for the group it was sorted into

typing.meaning: something that feeds into that answer

authored.reasoning: The ordinary consumer is the perspective the test is applied from, and a perspective is an input to the answer rather than a question in its own right. Typed alongside GC-0009 so the market and the consumer within it sit in the same group.
authored.expert_should_check: Whether examiners treat 'who is the ordinary consumer of these goods' as a question they decide, or as a standard they apply without deciding anything. The answer moves this record and probably GT-0009 with it.
alternatives_considered: legal_test — the Manual says in terms that 'the tests lie in the perception of the ordinary person', which can be read as making the ordinary consumer the test rather than a factor in it. The quote sits in this record's evidence precisely because it argues for the alternative.

evidence.quote: The tests lie in the perception of the ordinary person
That exceptionally stupid or careless consumers might be confused does not suffice.

nodes.label: surrounding circumstances
nodes.notes: The not_labels matter: Part 29.9.7 says expressly that the connotation must come from the mark itself and not from external considerations such as reputation in another mark. So "surrounding circumstances" is admissible and "external considerations" is not, and the two phrases look alike.

quote.text: In considering the probability of deception, all the surrounding circumstances have to be taken into consideration.
quote.from: the evidence for the group it was sorted into

typing.meaning: something that feeds into that answer

authored.reasoning: The clearest relevant_factor in the set: the corpus uses the words 'taken into consideration' and then lists what the category holds. Nothing is being decided and nothing is being taken out of the rule.
authored.expert_should_check: Whether the concept should survive as a single record at all, or be replaced by the particular circumstances the Manual lists. The typing is safe either way; the vocabulary question is not.
alternatives_considered: none_of_these — only if 'surrounding circumstances' is thought to be a container for factors rather than a factor, which would be a modelling objection rather than a legal one.

evidence.quote: In considering the probability of deception, all the surrounding circumstances have to be taken into consideration.
Surrounding circumstances include the manner in which the goods/services are purchased, the physical characteristics of goods and any other factor which would affect consumer perceptions.

nodes.label: specification of goods and services
nodes.notes: The Manual reasons about what a specification "notionally includes", which is a different thing from what the applicant sells.

quote.text: If, however, there is a connotation present within the trade mark that is directly contradicted by the specification, there is a high likelihood of consumers being deceived or confused.
quote.from: the evidence for the group it was sorted into

typing.meaning: something that feeds into that answer

authored.reasoning: The specification is one half of the comparison the whole of Part 29.4 turns on — connotation against claimed goods — so it feeds the deception answer directly. It is not itself decided and it does not take a case out of the rule.
authored.expert_should_check: Whether the specification as filed and the specification as amended are the same concept for typing purposes. This record and GT-0015 assume they are not.
alternatives_considered: exception — arguable on the PLATYPUS example, where a specification that matches the connotation means no ground is required. But that is the comparison coming out one way, not a carve-out from it; GC-0015 holds the carve-out and is typed exception.

evidence.quote: If, however, there is a connotation present within the trade mark that is directly contradicted by the specification, there is a high likelihood of consumers being deceived or confused.

If a trade mark contains an explicit claim about the goods which relates to a geographic location and that claim is not reflected in the specification or an endorsement, the trade mark is likely to deceive consumers if that claim turns out to be false.

nodes.label: condition of registration
nodes.notes: Whether an endorsement is the record of a condition or a separate thing is exactly the sort of tacit distinction this exercise is trying to surface.

quote.text: A section 43 ground for rejection may be overcome by the applicant agreeing to a condition of registration limiting use of the trade mark to goods containing the substance indicated by the relevant INN.
quote.from: the evidence for the group it was sorted into

typing.meaning: something that takes a case out of the rule

authored.reasoning: The corpus states it as the way a ground already made out is overcome, in both the INN and the geographical branches. A mechanism that removes a case from a ground it otherwise attracts is an exception on the owner's definition.
authored.expert_should_check: Whether 'overcoming a ground' and 'the ground not arising' are the same kind of thing. Four records — GT-0013, GT-0014, GT-0015, GT-0029 — are typed exception on the first, and GT-0020, GT-0027 and GT-0048 on the second.
alternatives_considered: none_of_these — a condition of registration is an administrative instrument, and the exception group may be meant for doctrinal carve-outs (GC-0027, GC-0048) rather than for remedies. On that reading GT-0013 to GT-0015 all move out of exception together and the group shrinks to five.

evidence.quote: A section 43 ground for rejection may be overcome by the applicant agreeing to a condition of registration limiting use of the trade mark to goods containing the substance indicated by the relevant INN.

An applicant will be able to overcome a geographical section 43 objection by agreeing to a condition of registration or a specification amendment which removes the likelihood of consumers being deceived or confused.

quote.text: The risk of deception can be mitigated by a suitably specific endorsement or an amendment or limitation to the specification of goods or services.
quote.from: the evidence for the group it was sorted into

typing.meaning: something that takes a case out of the rule

authored.reasoning: Typed with GC-0013 because Part 29.9.2 names the endorsement itself as mitigating the risk, not merely as the place where a condition is recorded. The lowest confidence in the exception group.
authored.expert_should_check: Whether an endorsement is a thing that does work or the writing-down of a thing that does. GC-0013's own record note flags this as exactly the kind of tacit distinction the exercise is meant to surface, and it is still open.
alternatives_considered: none_of_these — the reading to prefer if an endorsement is only the written record of a condition (GC-0013) or of a permission (GC-0029). On that view it is an artefact, does nothing of its own, and the two passages in the evidence are loose drafting rather than a separate mechanism.

evidence.quote: The risk of deception can be mitigated by a suitably specific endorsement or an amendment or limitation to the specification of goods or services.
Where permission is provided, this should be made clear by way of an endorsement.

nodes.label: limitation of the specification
nodes.notes: The second not_label is unsure: Part 12 discusses deleting goods and filing a divisional as related moves, and whether deletion is a limitation or something else is a practice question.

quote.text: An applicant will be able to overcome a geographical section 43 objection by agreeing to a condition of registration or a specification amendment which removes the likelihood of consumers being deceived or confused.
quote.from: the evidence for the group it was sorted into

typing.meaning: something that takes a case out of the rule

authored.reasoning: A limitation removes the likelihood of deception and so removes the ground, which is the exception group's definition applied literally. Part 29.9.5 goes further than the other two members of this trio by calling it the sole criterion for a limitation under s 43.
authored.expert_should_check: The same question as GT-0013: whether a remedy belongs in the exception group at all. If it does not, this record is relevant_factor and merges in substance with GT-0012.
alternatives_considered: relevant_factor — right if the limited specification is simply the specification (GC-0012) at a later moment, in which case what changes is the input and not the rule.

evidence.quote: An applicant will be able to overcome a geographical section 43 objection by agreeing to a condition of registration or a specification amendment which removes the likelihood of consumers being deceived or confused.
The risk of deception can be mitigated by a suitably specific endorsement or an amendment or limitation to the specification of goods or services.

nodes.label: priority date
nodes.notes: Whether the filing date and the priority date are distinct enough to be a not_label here is a practice question; they coincide in most applications and diverge in the ones that matter.

quote.text: Firstly, how well known is the person among relevant Australian consumers, as at the priority date?
quote.from: the evidence for the group it was sorted into

typing.meaning: something that feeds into that answer

authored.reasoning: The priority date fixes the moment at which how-well-known is measured, so it conditions the answer without being one. Typed relevant_factor as the temporal input to the well-known-person branch.
authored.expert_should_check: The tension GC-0049's note records: Part 29.3.2 directs attention to the current marketplace and Part 29.6 to the priority date. Both are typed relevant_factor here, which quietly asserts that they are two inputs rather than a contradiction.
alternatives_considered: none_of_these — right if a date is an administrative attribute of an application rather than something weighed. That reading is strengthened by the fact that the Manual mentions the priority date once in the whole of Part 29.

evidence.quote: Firstly, how well known is the person among relevant Australian consumers, as at the priority date?

nodes.label: geographical reference
nodes.notes: The first not_label is the important one: every geographical indication is a geographical reference and the reverse is false, and the two terms are used within a few paragraphs of each other.

quote.text: Trade marks which contain a geographical reference will often connote the geographical origin or some other attribute of goods or services.
quote.from: the evidence for the group it was sorted into

typing.meaning: something that feeds into that answer

authored.reasoning: The corpus is explicit that the mere presence of a place name demonstrates nothing automatically — it is material that feeds the connotation question and does not answer it. That sentence is the reason this whole family of subject-matter concepts is typed relevant_factor rather than ground_of_refusal.
authored.expert_should_check: The family judgement, once, rather than fifteen times: GT-0017 to GT-0023, GT-0025, GT-0026, GT-0030 to GT-0034, GT-0036 and GT-0037 are all typed relevant_factor because they name material rather than a reason to refuse. If that is wrong it is wrong for all of them.
alternatives_considered: ground_of_refusal — right if the four groups sort concepts by the rule they appear in rather than by the part they play in it. Fifteen records in this pass turn on the same choice.

evidence.quote: Trade marks which contain a geographical reference will often connote the geographical origin or some other attribute of goods or services.

the mere presence within a trade mark of a person's name, a descriptive term, a geographical place name or a reference to the size of packages or intended use of a product does not automatically demonstrate a connotation sufficient to trigger section 43

nodes.label: geographical indication
nodes.notes: The pilot area's material on GIs mostly points elsewhere — Part 29.1.1 sends the reader to Part 32B. Whether those destinations are in the pilot boundary is deliverable 1's question.

quote.text: If during examination of a new application research reveals that a trade mark is identical or similar to a listed EU GI, consideration should then be given to whether or not the use of the trade mark would potentially deceive or confuse Australian consumers and make grounds for rejection under s 43 appropriate.
quote.from: the evidence for the group it was sorted into

typing.meaning: something that feeds into that answer

authored.reasoning: The corpus makes a match against a listed EU GI the trigger for a further question rather than the answer to one — 'consideration should then be given to whether'. That is a factor by the owner's definition.
authored.expert_should_check: Whether the s 43 treatment of GIs is really in this vocabulary at all. GC-0018's own record note says Part 29.1.1 sends the reader to Part 32B, and the material this typing rests on is one paragraph about the EU agreement.
alternatives_considered: ground_of_refusal — the family alternative recorded at GT-0017.
none_of_these — right if a GI is treated as an external instrument the examiner consults rather than as a feature of the mark.

evidence.quote: If during examination of a new application research reveals that a trade mark is identical or similar to a listed EU GI, consideration should then be given to whether or not the use of the trade mark would potentially deceive or confuse Australian consumers and make grounds for rejection under s 43 appropriate.

quote.text: If a trade mark containing a geographical reference is found to connote geographical origin, consideration must then be given to whether ordinary consumers would be deceived or confused as a result.
quote.from: the evidence for the group it was sorted into

typing.meaning: something that feeds into that answer

authored.reasoning: Same structure as GT-0018 and stated in one sentence: origin is what the reference connotes, and the deception question is asked afterwards. The finding of origin is an input to that question.
authored.expert_should_check: Whether the geographical branch has its own connotation test, or whether it applies GC-0001's. This record assumes the second.
alternatives_considered: legal_test — 'is the mark found to connote geographical origin' is arguably a question the examiner answers, which would make this the geographical branch's version of GC-0001.

evidence.quote: If a trade mark containing a geographical reference is found to connote geographical origin, consideration must then be given to whether ordinary consumers would be deceived or confused as a result.

nodes.label: business identifier
nodes.notes: The Manual's examples both contain place names, which is what makes this a genuine trap rather than a distinction on paper.

quote.text: Where business identifiers are included in a trade mark (e.g. A TASMANIAN COMPANY, RIVERINA DAIRY CO.) this tends to indicate a characteristic of a business rather than the goods or services themselves. A ground for rejection will rarely apply in these cases.
quote.from: the evidence for the group it was sorted into

typing.meaning: something that takes a case out of the rule

authored.reasoning: The only member of the geographical family the corpus carves out: a place name inside a business identifier is read as saying something about the business, and the ground will rarely apply. That is a case taken out of the rule.
authored.expert_should_check: Whether 'will rarely apply' is practice-speak for an exception or an honest statement of frequency. The distinction decides this record and nothing else.
alternatives_considered: relevant_factor — 'rarely' is not 'never', so this may be a strong factor against a connotation rather than an exception to the ground. That reading would put it back with GT-0017 and leave the exception group without a geographical member other than GT-0048.

evidence.quote: Where business identifiers are included in a trade mark (e.g. A TASMANIAN COMPANY, RIVERINA DAIRY CO.) this tends to indicate a characteristic of a business rather than the goods or services themselves. A ground for rejection will rarely apply in these cases.

nodes.label: geographical qualifier
nodes.notes: Whether "made in" and "product of" are labels for this concept or examples of it is a modelling choice, not a legal one — but it changes how the entity annotations attach.

quote.text: are not necessary for a connotation to be present in a mark
quote.from: the evidence for the group it was sorted into

typing.meaning: something that feeds into that answer

authored.reasoning: A qualifier strengthens a geographical claim into an explicit one, and the corpus says its absence does not defeat a connotation. Something that makes a finding more or less likely without settling it is a factor.
authored.expert_should_check: Whether this concept survives at all. If it is a list of example phrases rather than an idea, the typing is beside the point and the record should be withdrawn instead.
alternatives_considered: none_of_these — right if 'made in' and 'product of' are examples of GC-0017 rather than a concept in their own right, which GC-0021's own record note raises as a live modelling question.

evidence.quote: are not necessary for a connotation to be present in a mark

If a trade mark contains an explicit claim about the goods which relates to a geographic location and that claim is not reflected in the specification or an endorsement, the trade mark is likely to deceive consumers if that claim turns out to be false.

nodes.label: International Non-Proprietary Name
alt: generic name for a pharmaceutical substance
nodes.notes: The first not_label is the whole difficulty of Part 29.5: an INN and an INN stem are governed by different rules and named almost identically.

quote.text: A ground for rejection under section 43 exists where a trade mark, or part of a trade mark, to be used in relation to pharmaceuticals or veterinary substances is the same as, or may connote, a notified INN and use of the trade mark in respect of the goods covered by the specification are not restricted to the particular substance indicated by the INN.
quote.from: the evidence for the group it was sorted into

typing.meaning: something that feeds into that answer

authored.reasoning: An INN is a name maintained by the WHO. Whether a mark is or connotes one is the input; the ground arises from that plus an unrestricted specification. Typed with the rest of the subject-matter family.
authored.expert_should_check: Whether the vocabulary needs a concept for the compound condition — 'mark connotes an INN and specification is unrestricted' — as distinct from the INN itself. Without one the ground_of_refusal group stays nearly empty.
alternatives_considered: ground_of_refusal — the family alternative at GT-0017, and unusually strong here because Part 29.5.4 opens with the words 'A ground for rejection under section 43 exists where'. What follows those words is a compound condition, of which the INN is one part.

evidence.quote: A ground for rejection under section 43 exists where a trade mark, or part of a trade mark, to be used in relation to pharmaceuticals or veterinary substances is the same as, or may connote, a notified INN and use of the trade mark in respect of the goods covered by the specification are not restricted to the particular substance indicated by the INN.
IP Australia is aware of the need to prevent use of INNs (and words that may connote an INN) in a manner that is likely to deceive or cause confusion

nodes.label: INN stem
nodes.notes: "Prefix" and "suffix" are listed as not_labels because the Manual uses them to describe a stem's *position*, not as names for it — a stem can be a prefix, a suffix or an infix.

quote.text: improper use of an INN stem in a trade mark may lead to deception or confusion
quote.from: the evidence for the group it was sorted into

typing.meaning: something that feeds into that answer

authored.reasoning: 'May lead to' is the language of a factor, and the stem's presence is only the start of the enquiry — GC-0024 holds the question that follows it. Typed relevant_factor with the INN itself.
authored.expert_should_check: Whether an INN and an INN stem should type the same way at all. They are governed by different rules and named almost identically, which GC-0022's record note calls the whole difficulty of Part 29.5.

edges.text: The application of section 43 is, by the wording of the section, mandatory.
There is, therefore, no discretion to accept a trade mark that is caught by the provisions of this section.

However for a trade mark to be caught by these provisions it is necessary for a decision maker to be clearly satisfied that use of the trade mark for the specified goods and / or services would be likely to deceive or cause confusion.
A connotation must arise from the trade mark itself, and not through a comparison with another trade mark.
A connotation may result from the whole trade mark or from a part of the trade mark.
It may result from a dictionary meaning or from a connection in the minds of the buying public with some person, place or thing.
The Registrar must be satisfied that a ground for rejection exists before section 33(3) can be applied to reject the trade mark.
If there is doubt that a connotation exists, then the ground for rejection should not be raised.

For a trade mark to trigger section 43 there must be some connotation within the trade mark that would reasonably be expected to cause deception or confusion in the mind of the relevant buying public.

However, the mere presence within a trade mark of a person's name, a descriptive term, a geographical place name or a reference to the size of packages or intended use of a product does not automatically demonstrate a connotation sufficient to trigger section 43.
For a ground for rejection to be raised the connotation must be obvious, direct, and immediate and within the trade mark itself.
The prominence and context of the potentially deceptive or confusing element in the trade mark will be important in deciding whether the trade mark is likely to deceive or cause confusion.
There must be a real and obvious danger of the buying public being deceived and/or confused by the secondary meaning within the trade mark.
Each application must be considered as it stands in the current marketplace, not in the marketplace as it was in the past and not as it may be in the future.
A sign regarded as deceptive or confusing under the previous legislation may no longer have the same connotation and a ground for rejection may not apply under the current Act.

In some cases a connotation giving rise to a section 43 ground for rejection may not be obvious during examination and will only emerge at opposition when the full facts of a case are available to the decision maker.

A section 43 ground for rejection may be overcome by the applicant agreeing to a condition of registration limiting use of the trade mark to goods containing the substance indicated by the relevant INN.

A section 43 ground for rejection may be overcome by the applicant agreeing to a condition of registration limiting use of the trade mark to goods containing substances belonging to the relevant INN stem.
Some INN stems consist of simple two or three letter combinations and their presence in a larger word may not be meaningful and as a result would not lead to deception or confusion.
Claims for specific pharmaceutical or veterinary goods in Class 5 may also trigger the provisions of section 43 in relation to INNs and INN stems.
If a trade mark contains a name of a person (or group of people) which is well known in relation to the specified goods or services, the provisions of section 43 may be triggered.
An applicant may overcome a section 43 ground for rejection in relation to a name by providing the well-known person’s written permission to use their name as a trade mark.

The more common the name, whether it is a given name, surname, or combination of both, the less likely consumers will be to make this assumption, as many well-known people have names shared by many other people.
A section 43 ground for rejection should not be raised merely because a trade mark contains the image of a person.

However, a relevant connotation may arise if the deceased person’s estate (or other authorised entity) has continued to control the use of the person’s name/image after their death, e.g. by commercialising directly or licensing to third parties.

Other phone numbers which do not appear to represent a phoneword should not be queried or researched specifically in respect of section 43, unless other information before the examiner gives them particular reason to suspect that the applicant may not be the licensed user of the number.

Examiners will also need to consider raising a section 41 ground for rejection in relation to any trade mark which could viewed as a radio call sign or frequency that simply consists of that material or with other descriptive or non distinctive elements.
The same considerations apply to services as to goods, though careful consideration needs to be given to circumstances which may mitigate the risk of deception or confusion.
The condition of registration or specification amendment must directly address the connotation in the trade mark.

If a trade mark, or some part of the trade mark, contains a reference to Indigenous people and a connotation arises from the mark that would be likely to deceive or confuse consumers within the relevant market, then a ground for rejection under s43 should be raised.

If during examination of a new application research reveals that a trade mark is identical or similar to a listed EU GI, consideration should then be given to whether or not the use of the trade mark would potentially deceive or confuse Australian consumers and make grounds for rejection under s 43 appropriate.

groups.meaning: an act, proceeding or event that moves an application or a registration from one state to the next

groups.label: Instrument or record
groups.meaning: a document, entry or endorsement the process produces, or writes to the Register

groups.label: External instrument
groups.meaning: a treaty or international scheme Australian practice adopts, rather than a rule the Act itself makes

groups.label: None of these
groups.meaning: none of the nine fit — which is an answer, not a gap

edgeKinds.label: contains
edgeKinds.meaning: One concept sits under another, as the record's own `broader` / `narrower` fields state it.

edgeKinds.label: related to
edgeKinds.meaning: The two concepts are recorded as related — an associative link, not a hierarchy.

edgeKinds.label: asserted
edgeKinds.meaning: A signed `GR-` relationship record: a named reviewer wrote this edge, with the passage it rests on and a modality.

edgeKinds.label: cites
edgeKinds.meaning: The concept's record names this provision as its legislative basis.

blocks.title: What an edge on this map is, and what it is not
blocks.text: Four things put an edge here, and all four are already written down in a record: a `broader` / `narrower` pair, a `related` pair, a signed **relationship** record, and a concept naming the provision it rests on. **Nothing on this canvas was inferred, and no edge means one idea implies another.** The thin ones are vocabulary structure; the thick ones are the 31 a reviewer put their name to, and those are the only ones carrying a modality and a passage.

blocks.title: The shape of this picture is itself the finding
blocks.text: The graph is in **44 separate pieces**. One of them holds 86 nodes and is the signed vocabulary with its hierarchy and its 35 asserted edges; almost every other piece is a single authored concept with the provisions it cites and nothing else. `authored/relationships.yaml` does not exist, so what the rows below the core show is a **vocabulary drawn next to a graph**, not a graph. Writing those edges is the largest single piece of work still to do, and this picture is what it would change.
